research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. What `java.security.KeyPairGenerator` governs, and what the finding refers to

`java.security.KeyPairGenerator` is the JCA engine class for generating public/private key pairs for a selected algorithm; the generated keys carry algorithm-specific parameters. Instances are obtained through `getInstance(...)`, optionally initialized, and then used to generate a `KeyPair`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

The reported text:

> expecting one of RSA,EC,DSA,DiffieHellman,DH but found Ed25519

refers to the **algorithm value bound at the rule’s `getInstance(algorithm)` / `getInstance(algorithm, _)` event**, not to the returned `KeyPair`, a key encoding, or a key-size argument. The cited CrySL source applies the direct constraint:

> `algorithm in {"RSA", "EC", "DSA", "DiffieHellman", "DH"};`

Thus, an `Ed25519` string does not satisfy this rule-pack allowlist. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

This is **not an API-level assertion that `Ed25519` is invalid for `KeyPairGenerator`**. Oracle’s Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification explicitly lists `Ed25519` as a `KeyPairGenerator` algorithm for Ed25519 Edwards-curve signature key pairs. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

### 2. Documented Java usage and documented remediation

The official `KeyPairGenerator` API documents these usage semantics:

- Obtain an instance with `getInstance(String algorithm)` or a provider-selecting overload. Without a selected provider, the API uses the first registered provider supporting the algorithm; if no provider supports it, `getInstance` throws `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
- Initialize either with:
  - an algorithm-independent integer key size, optionally with `SecureRandom`; or
  - an algorithm-specific `AlgorithmParameterSpec`, optionally with `SecureRandom`.  
  Key size is an algorithm-specific metric, and an unsupported value causes `InvalidParameterException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
- Generate a fresh pair with `generateKeyPair()` or its `genKeyPair()` alias. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
- If initialization is omitted, providers must supply and document defaults. Those defaults may vary by provider and may change in a later release. The API therefore **recommends explicit initialization rather than reliance on provider defaults**. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

The Java API does **not** document the CrySL allowlist `{RSA, EC, DSA, DiffieHellman, DH}`, label `Ed25519` unsafe, or recommend replacing `Ed25519` with one of those algorithms. Its only directly relevant documented remediation recommendation is explicit initialization when provider-dependent defaults would otherwise be used. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

For Oracle JDK 15’s `SunEC` provider specifically, `Ed25519`, `Ed448`, and `EdDSA` appear as supported `KeyPairGenerator` algorithms. Its documented Ed25519 integer initialization restriction is a key size of 255 bits; this is provider documentation, not a cross-provider JCA guarantee. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/security/security-developer-guide.pdf))

### 3. Compatibility: persisted material, wire formats, platform support, and migration

**Persisted key material and encodings.** The JCA standard-names specification identifies `X.509` as the ASN.1 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` public-key format and `PKCS#8` as the ASN.1 `PrivateKeyInfo` private-key format. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html)) For Ed25519 specifically, RFC 8410 defines the Ed25519 algorithm identifier/OID and specifies its use in public-key, private-key, certificate, and signature structures. In particular, an X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` carries an `AlgorithmIdentifier`, and Ed25519 has its own OID (`1.3.101.112`). ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8410.html))

Accordingly, the official sources establish that algorithm identity is part of common encoded/certificate structures. They do **not** document any generic conversion of an existing RSA, EC, DSA, or DH key pair into an Ed25519 key pair, nor a generic preservation of key bytes, certificates, signatures, or peer interoperability after changing key algorithms. Compatibility depends on the particular persisted-key consumer, certificate profile, protocol/wire format, peer capability, provider, and signature or key-agreement operation. That information is outside `KeyPairGenerator` itself.

**Wire formats.** `KeyPairGenerator` does not define a network protocol or wire format. RFC 8410 covers Ed25519 identifiers and encodings in X.509/PKIX-related ASN.1 structures, but it is not a general migration procedure for every application protocol. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8410.html))

**Platform/provider support.** The Oracle JDK 15 documentation shows both Ed25519 key-spec APIs “Since: 15” and `SunEC` support for the Ed25519 `KeyPairGenerator` service. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/EdECPrivateKeySpec.html)) Current Java SE standard-name documentation also recognizes `Ed25519` as a `KeyPairGenerator` algorithm. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html)) However, the `KeyPairGenerator` class documentation’s mandatory-algorithm list does not list Ed25519 among the algorithms every Java-platform implementation must support. Therefore, availability must be checked for the actual Java runtime and selected provider; standard naming alone is not a universal availability guarantee. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

**Documented migration path.** No `KeyPairGenerator` API source located documents an algorithm-migration path for persisted keys, certificates, or protocol peers. The documented API guidance is limited to factory selection, provider support, initialization, and generation. This leaves the relevant key consumers and their accepted algorithms/formats unresolved.

### 4. Exact CrySL source rule

**Direct source URL:**  
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl

The source declares the governed receiver type at the specification level as `java.security.KeyPairGenerator`. It does not declare a separate receiver expression on each event. Its matching clause is:

```text
SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator

OBJECTS
	java.lang.String algorithm;
	java.security.KeyPair keyPair;
	java.security.spec.AlgorithmParameterSpec params;
	int keysize;

EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(algorithm);
	g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: initialize(keysize);
	i2: initialize(keysize, _);
	i3: initialize(params);
	i4: initialize(params, _);
	Init := i1 | i2 | i3 | i4;

	k1: keyPair = generateKeyPair();
	k2: keyPair = genKeyPair();
	Gen := k1 | k2;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

From that text:

- **Receiver/API type:** the specification is explicitly for `java.security.KeyPairGenerator`.
- **Matched method names:** `getInstance`, `initialize`, `generateKeyPair`, and `genKeyPair`.
- **Parameter-list constraint:** yes. The source distinguishes one- and two-argument forms of `getInstance` and `initialize`; it binds the first argument as `algorithm`, `keysize`, or `params` as applicable. It uses `_` for the second argument and does not state that argument’s type in the CrySL file itself. `generateKeyPair()` and `genKeyPair()` are zero-argument events and bind the result to `keyPair`.
- **Order:** `Get, Init, Gen`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))
- **Condition evaluated for this finding:** the algorithm allowlist quoted above. The source additionally contains algorithm-dependent key-size constraints and required `prepared*` predicates for parameter-spec initialization. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

**Can it match a method that merely shares a governed API method name?** **No, not as this specification is written.** The source is scoped to the fully qualified API type `java.security.KeyPairGenerator`; it does not state a name-only or global match over arbitrary receiver types. The file itself does not provide further implementation-level matcher semantics beyond that `SPEC` declaration and the listed event patterns. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

### Source limitations and unresolved points

- The provided CrySL URL is on the repository’s moving `master` branch. The supplied material does not identify the exact Crypto-API-Rules commit or CryptoAnalysis version that produced the reported result, so equivalence between the retrieved rule text and the detector’s executed version cannot be established from these sources alone.
- The supplied report does not identify the selected provider, runtime Java version, actual initialization overload or arguments, generated-key consumer, persisted format, or protocol. Those facts are required to determine provider availability and compatibility details.
- The CrySL constraint result is distinct from Java API runtime validity: Oracle’s standard-name documentation recognizes `Ed25519` for `KeyPairGenerator`, while the retrieved CrySL rule excludes it from its own allowlist. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))
